summary: Zotepine is an atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic of the dibenzothiepine class, used for the treatment of schizophrenia. It is NOT approved by the US FDA; it has been licensed in the United Kingdom, parts of Europe, and Japan, so the information here is drawn from the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) and BNF rather than an FDA label. It antagonises dopamine D1 and D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A/2C receptors, inhibits noradrenaline reuptake, and blocks histamine H1 and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. The usual adult starting dose is 25 mg three times daily, titrated as needed up to a maximum of 100 mg three times daily (300 mg/day); elderly patients start at a lower dose with a lower maximum. Zotepine causes dose-dependent QT-interval prolongation and a dose-dependent lowering of the seizure threshold, so ECG monitoring is advised and it should be avoided in patients with a history of seizures or significant QT prolongation. Like other atypical antipsychotics it can cause weight gain, hyperglycaemia/diabetes, dyslipidaemia, sedation, and hyperprolactinaemia.

dosage.d: Initial 25 mg three times daily; titrate at intervals of about 4 days up to 100 mg three times daily; maximum 300 mg/day
dosage.t: Use the lowest effective dose; titrate slowly to limit QT and seizure risk

dosage.d: Start 25 mg twice daily; titrate cautiously; usual maximum 75 mg three times daily
dosage.t: Increased sensitivity; greater risk of hypotension and sedation
dosage.n: Avoid in dementia-related psychosis (increased mortality/stroke risk with antipsychotics)

admin: Take orally, usually three times daily, with or without food
Titrate the dose slowly to minimise QT prolongation and seizure risk
Obtain a baseline ECG and electrolytes; recheck the ECG during dose increases
Avoid abrupt discontinuation; withdraw gradually to reduce rebound/withdrawal symptoms
Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants
Use a lower dose and slower titration in the elderly and in renal or hepatic impairment
moa: Zotepine is an antagonist at dopamine D1 and D2 receptors and at serotonin 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors; the combined D2/5-HT2A blockade is characteristic of atypical antipsychotics and is thought to relieve positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia while reducing the liability for extrapyramidal effects compared with typical agents. It also inhibits the reuptake of noradrenaline. Antagonism of histamine H1 receptors contributes to sedation and weight gain, and blockade of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors contributes to orthostatic hypotension. Its dose-related blockade of cardiac potassium channels underlies QT prolongation, and the molecule lowers the seizure threshold in a dose-dependent manner.

absolute: Acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics, or psychotropic drugs (CNS depression)
Acute gout or history of nephrolithiasis (zotepine can raise uric acid) - per SmPC
Concomitant use with drugs that markedly prolong the QT interval
relative: History of seizures or epilepsy (dose-dependent seizure threshold lowering)
QT prolongation, significant cardiac disease, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia)
Diabetes mellitus or risk factors for metabolic syndrome
Prostatic hypertrophy, narrow-angle glaucoma, paralytic ileus (anticholinergic/antiadrenergic effects)
Elderly, particularly with dementia (increased mortality/stroke risk)
monitor: Weight/BMI, fasting glucose, HbA1c, and lipids
Signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome and extrapyramidal symptoms

preg: There are limited human data; zotepine should be avoided in pregnancy unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk. Neonates exposed to antipsychotics during the third trimester are at risk of extrapyramidal and withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia or hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, feeding difficulty, respiratory distress) that may vary in severity and duration. If used, monitor the neonate.
lact: Zotepine and its metabolites are likely excreted in breast milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse effects in a nursing infant, breastfeeding should generally be avoided during treatment.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; plasma levels may be increased. Use lower starting doses and slower titration, and monitor for sedation, hypotension, and QT effects.
hepatic: Zotepine is extensively metabolised by the liver. Use with caution in hepatic impairment, with lower doses and careful titration; avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

major: QT-prolonging drugs - class IA/III antiarrhythmics, other antipsychotics, certain antibiotics (macrolides, fluoroquinolones), antifungals, methadone, ondansetron (additive QT prolongation / torsades)
Drugs lowering the seizure threshold and CNS depressants (additive seizure risk and sedation)
Drugs causing electrolyte disturbance, e.g. potassium-depleting diuretics (potentiate QT risk)
moderate: CYP enzyme inhibitors (e.g. fluoxetine, diazepam reported to raise zotepine levels)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive CNS depression and sedation
interactions.diagnostics: Can prolong the QT interval on ECG, raise prolactin, glucose, lipids, hepatic transaminases, and uric acid

serious: QT-interval prolongation and ventricular arrhythmia (torsades de pointes)
emergency: Torsades de pointes / serious ventricular arrhythmia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability)

monitoring: ECG (QT interval) at baseline and during dose titration; serum electrolytes
Weight/BMI, waist circumference, fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipids at baseline and periodically
Blood pressure (including orthostatic) particularly during titration
Extrapyramidal symptoms and signs of tardive dyskinesia
Full blood count if signs of infection or fever (rare agranulocytosis)
counsel: Take this medicine exactly as prescribed and do not stop it suddenly - tell your doctor before stopping
It can make you drowsy and dizzy, especially when standing up; rise slowly and avoid driving until you know how it affects you
Report fainting, palpitations, or an irregular heartbeat - this drug can affect heart rhythm
Tell your doctor if you have ever had fits/seizures; this medicine can make seizures more likely
Watch for weight gain and increased thirst/urination; you will have blood tests for sugar and cholesterol
Seek urgent care for high fever with muscle stiffness and confusion (a rare serious reaction)
pk: Antipsychotic effect develops over days to weeks of regular dosing
Peak plasma concentration about 2 to 4 hours after an oral dose
Parent drug approximately 14-16 hours; active metabolite (norzotepine) longer
Store at controlled room temperature (about 15-25 degrees C); protect from moisture and light
pearls: Zotepine is NOT FDA-approved - this record is based on the EU/UK SmPC and BNF; verify against local labelling before prescribing.
It causes dose-dependent QT-interval prolongation - obtain a baseline ECG, correct electrolytes, avoid other QT-prolonging drugs, and monitor.
It lowers the seizure threshold in a dose-dependent fashion - avoid in patients with a history of seizures and titrate slowly.
Expect metabolic effects (weight gain, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia) and hyperprolactinaemia; monitor weight, glucose, and lipids.
Start low and go slow, especially in the elderly (max ~75 mg three times daily) and in hepatic/renal impairment.
Like all antipsychotics, it increases mortality and stroke risk in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis - avoid this use.
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your usual three-times-daily schedule - do not take a double dose. If several doses are missed, contact your doctor, as the dose may need to be re-titrated.
overdose: Overdose may cause drowsiness, marked sedation, hypotension, tachycardia, extrapyramidal symptoms, seizures, QT prolongation with cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory depression, and coma. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive: protect the airway, monitor cardiac rhythm (continuous ECG) and vital signs, correct electrolytes, treat hypotension with fluids and pressors (avoiding drugs with beta-agonist activity such as adrenaline because of unopposed alpha effects/hypotension), control seizures with benzodiazepines, and treat arrhythmias. Activated charcoal may be considered for recent ingestion; dialysis is not expected to be useful given high protein binding.
